original: Damlaya damlaya göl olur.
literal: Drop by drop, it becomes a lake.
meanings: Small amounts add up to something big over time
Little efforts accumulate into great results
Saving a little at a time builds up a lot
Small things add up
Saving bit by bit adds up
Little by little you build something big
Many small efforts make a big result
englishEquivalent: Every little helps. / Many a little makes a mickle.
englishEquivalents: Every little helps
Many a little makes a mickle
Little strokes fell great oaks
hints: Think about what happens when you keep adding something tiny, again and again.
It is often said to encourage saving money or steady work.
It's about how small things, repeated, add up to something large.

original: 猿も木から落ちる
literal: Even monkeys fall from trees.
meanings: Even experts make mistakes
Everyone, however skilled, sometimes fails
Nobody is perfect, not even the best at something
Everyone makes mistakes
Even the best can get it wrong
Experts slip up too
No one is so skilled that they never fail
englishEquivalent: Even Homer nods. / Nobody's perfect.
englishEquivalents: Even Homer nods
Nobody is perfect
To err is human
hints: Climbing trees is what monkeys are best at.
It's said to comfort someone who slipped up at their own speciality.
It's about how even the most skilled people get things wrong.

original: Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente.
literal: The shrimp that falls asleep is carried away by the current.
meanings: If you are not alert, you will miss out or fall behind
If you are lazy or careless, events will sweep you away
Stay attentive or others will get ahead of you
Stay alert or you will miss out
If you are lazy you will lose out
Don’t get complacent or you will be left behind
Opportunities pass you by if you are not paying attention
englishEquivalent: You snooze, you lose.
englishEquivalents: You snooze, you lose
hints: What does the shrimp lose by sleeping?
It's a warning to people who are slow to act or not paying attention.
It's about missing out because you weren't alert.

original: بندر کیا جانے ادرک کا سواد
literal: What does a monkey know of the taste of ginger?
meanings: An ignorant person cannot appreciate something valuable
Some people cannot appreciate quality or refinement
You can't expect someone without taste to value fine things
Fools cannot appreciate good things
Some people don’t know the value of what they have
An ignorant person can’t recognise quality
Wasting something valuable on someone who doesn’t understand it
englishEquivalent: Casting pearls before swine.
englishEquivalents: Casting pearls before swine
hints: Ginger is prized, but a monkey would just spit it out.
It's said, usually with a sneer, about someone who doesn't value what they're given.
It's about people who can't appreciate something good.

original: Η γλώσσα κόκαλα δεν έχει και κόκαλα τσακίζει.
literal: The tongue has no bones, yet it breaks bones.
meanings: Words can cause great harm
What you say can hurt people deeply
Speech is powerful and can be very damaging
Words can hurt
Harsh words can do real damage
Be careful what you say because words wound
Saying hurtful things can be as bad as violence
englishEquivalent: Words can cut deeper than knives.
englishEquivalents: Words can cut deeper than knives
hints: The tongue here stands for something it produces.
It's a warning to be careful how you speak to people.
It's about how words can wound as badly as violence.

original: Usipoziba ufa utajenga ukuta.
literal: If you don't fill the crack, you will have to build a wall.
meanings: Fix small problems early before they become big ones
Neglecting a minor issue leads to a much bigger job later
Dealing with trouble early saves a lot of effort
Fix problems while they are small
Deal with problems before they get worse
Small issues become big issues if ignored
Prevention is easier than repair
englishEquivalent: A stitch in time saves nine.
englishEquivalents: A stitch in time saves nine
Nip it in the bud
hints: Compare how much work a crack takes with how much a whole wall takes.
It's advice about timing and neglect.
It's about fixing small problems before they grow.

original: 画蛇添足
literal: Drawing a snake and adding feet to it.
meanings: Adding something unnecessary spoils what was already finished
Overdoing something ruins it
Knowing when to stop, because extra effort can make things worse
Do not overdo it
Adding unnecessary things ruins it
Leave it alone once it is finished
Doing too much can spoil a good thing
englishEquivalent: Gilding the lily. / Leave well enough alone.
englishEquivalents: Gilding the lily
Leave well enough alone
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it
hints: Does a snake need feet?
The drawing was already complete before the feet went on.
It's about ruining something by adding what isn't needed.

original: Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid.
literal: Little by little, the bird builds its nest.
meanings: Patience and steady effort achieve big goals
Great things are built gradually, one small step at a time
Keep working slowly and you will get there
Be patient, progress comes slowly
Big goals are reached through small steady steps
Patience and persistence pay off
Slow progress still gets you there
englishEquivalent: Rome wasn't built in a day.
englishEquivalents: Rome wasn’t built in a day
hints: A nest is made one twig at a time.
It's said to someone frustrated by slow progress.
It's about patience and gradual effort paying off.

original: مار گزیده از ریسمان سیاه و سفید می‌ترسد
literal: Someone bitten by a snake is afraid of a black-and-white rope.
meanings: After a bad experience, people become fearful of anything similar
Past harm makes you overly cautious
Once hurt, you fear even harmless things that remind you of it
Bad experiences make you fearful
Once hurt, you become overly cautious
People who were harmed before are scared of anything similar
A bad experience makes you fear things that remind you of it
englishEquivalent: Once bitten, twice shy.
englishEquivalents: Once bitten, twice shy
A burnt child dreads the fire
hints: A striped rope can look a bit like a snake.
The rope is harmless; the fear comes from memory.
It's about becoming wary after being hurt once.

original: Ăn quả nhớ kẻ trồng cây.
literal: When you eat the fruit, remember the one who planted the tree.
meanings: Be grateful to those who made your good fortune possible
Remember and appreciate the people whose work came before you
Show gratitude for what others have given you
Be grateful
Appreciate the people who made your life possible
Don’t forget who helped you
Thank those who came before you
englishEquivalent: Don't forget those who paved the way.
englishEquivalents: Don’t bite the hand that feeds you
hints: Someone else did the work long before the fruit was ready.
It's often said about parents, teachers and ancestors.
It's about gratitude.

original: Üzüm üzüme baka baka kararır.
literal: A grape darkens by looking at another grape.
meanings: People become like the company they keep
You pick up the habits of those around you
Friends and surroundings influence who you become
You become like your friends
You are influenced by the people around you
Bad company can change you for the worse
People copy the habits of their friends
englishEquivalent: You are the company you keep.
englishEquivalents: You are the company you keep
Birds of a feather flock together
One bad apple spoils the bunch
hints: Grapes on the same bunch ripen together.
It's often said about children and their friends.
It's about becoming like the people around you.

original: Nie chwal dnia przed zachodem słońca.
literal: Don't praise the day before the sun has set.
meanings: Don't celebrate success until it is certain
Wait until something is finished before judging it a success
Things can still go wrong, so don't be overconfident too early
Do not celebrate too early
Don’t count on success until it’s over
Wait until the end before celebrating
Don’t be overconfident before you finish
englishEquivalent: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
englishEquivalents: Don’t count your chickens before they hatch
It ain’t over till it’s over
hints: A lot can still happen before evening.
It's a warning against premature confidence.
It's about not celebrating until something is truly over.

original: 낮말은 새가 듣고 밤말은 쥐가 듣는다
literal: Birds hear the words spoken by day, and mice hear the words spoken by night.
meanings: Be careful what you say, because someone is always listening
Secrets get out; you are never truly unheard
Watch your words, as they can reach unexpected ears
Someone is always listening
Be careful what you say, someone may overhear
There are no real secrets
Gossip always gets around
englishEquivalent: Walls have ears.
englishEquivalents: Walls have ears
hints: Whatever the time of day, something is listening.
It's a warning given to gossips.
It's about being careful what you say, because it can be overheard.

original: دور کے ڈھول سہانے
literal: Drums sound pleasant from far away.
meanings: Things seem better from a distance than they really are
Something unfamiliar looks more attractive than it is up close
Other places and situations always seem better than your own
Things look better from far away
What you don’t have always seems better
Distance makes things look more attractive than they are
Things seem better until you experience them yourself
englishEquivalent: The grass is always greener on the other side.
englishEquivalents: The grass is always greener on the other side
hints: Imagine standing right next to the drummer instead.
It's said to people dreaming about a life somewhere else.
It's about things looking better from a distance.

original: Água mole em pedra dura, tanto bate até que fura.
literal: Soft water on hard stone keeps striking until it makes a hole.
meanings: Persistence overcomes even the hardest obstacles
Keep trying and you will eventually succeed
Gentle but constant effort can wear down anything
Persistence pays off
Persistence wins in the end
Never give up and you will eventually break through
Constant effort beats any obstacle
englishEquivalent: Constant dripping wears away the stone.
englishEquivalents: If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again
hints: Water is weak; what makes it win?
It's said to encourage someone who keeps failing.
It's about persistence beating resistance.

original: اللي إيده في المية مش زي اللي إيده في النار
literal: The one whose hand is in the water is not like the one whose hand is in the fire.
meanings: Someone in comfort can't understand the suffering of someone in trouble
It's easy to judge when you aren't the one facing the hardship
People who aren't affected don't feel the pain of those who are
You cannot understand someone else’s pain unless you feel it
Only the one suffering truly understands the pain
It’s easy to give advice when you are not the one in trouble
Those who are comfortable can’t understand those who struggle
englishEquivalent: Easy for you to say. / Walk a mile in my shoes.

Walk a mile in someone else’s shoes
hints: One hand is comfortable, the other is in pain.
It's said in reply to unwanted advice from someone who isn't affected.
It's about how people who aren't suffering can't truly understand those who are.

original: 急がば回れ
literal: If you are in a hurry, take the long way round.
meanings: Taking the slower, safer route is often faster in the end
Rushing leads to mistakes, so be careful even when in a hurry
Haste causes delays; the careful way gets you there sooner
Rushing makes things slower
Rushing causes mistakes
Being careful is quicker than hurrying
Slow down to get there sooner
englishEquivalent: More haste, less speed.
englishEquivalents: More haste, less speed
Haste makes waste
hints: The shortcut might be risky or blocked.
It's advice for anyone tempted to cut corners.
It's about how rushing often ends up slowing you down.

original: Is minic a bhris béal duine a shrón.
literal: It is often a person's mouth that has broken their nose.
meanings: Talking too much or saying the wrong thing gets you into trouble
Your own careless words can bring harm on yourself

Your words can get you into trouble

Saying the wrong thing can get you hurt
Keep quiet to stay out of trouble
englishEquivalent: Loose lips sink ships. / Think before you speak.
englishEquivalents: Think before you speak
Me and my big mouth
hints: Whose fist really caused the broken nose?
It's a warning to someone who can't keep quiet.
It's about how what you say can come back to hurt you.

original: น้ำขึ้นให้รีบตัก
literal: When the water rises, hurry to scoop it up.
meanings: Take advantage of opportunities while they last
Act quickly when conditions are favourable
Seize the moment before the chance passes
Seize opportunities while you can
Make the most of a good chance while it lasts
Act fast when the opportunity comes
Take advantage of good times while you can
englishEquivalent: Make hay while the sun shines.
englishEquivalents: Make hay while the sun shines
Strike while the iron is hot
hints: High water won't stay high forever.
It's about timing.
It's about seizing an opportunity before it disappears.

original: اب پچھتائے کیا ہوت جب چڑیاں چگ گئیں کھیت
literal: What use is regret now, when the birds have already eaten the field?
meanings: It's pointless to regret something after the damage is done
Act in time, because regret afterwards cannot fix anything
Once the chance is gone, regretting it is useless
Regret is useless when it is too late
It’s too late to regret it now
Regret doesn’t undo the damage
You should have acted before it was too late
englishEquivalent: It's no use crying over spilt milk.
englishEquivalents: It’s no use crying over spilt milk
Shutting the stable door after the horse has bolted
hints: The farmer should have guarded the field earlier.
It's said to someone lamenting a mistake that can't be undone.
It's about how regret is useless once it's too late.

original: Dost acı söyler.
literal: A friend speaks bitter words.
meanings: A true friend tells you the hard truth
Real friends are honest even when it hurts
Someone who cares about you will tell you unpleasant truths
True friends tell you the truth
A real friend is honest with you
Friends tell you what you need to hear, not what you want to hear
Honest criticism comes from people who care
englishEquivalent: Faithful are the wounds of a friend.
englishEquivalents: Faithful are the wounds of a friend
The truth hurts
hints: Bitter here means unpleasant to hear, not angry.
A flatterer would tell you only what you want to hear.
It's about honesty being a sign of real friendship.

original: Tra il dire e il fare c’è di mezzo il mare.
literal: Between saying and doing, there is the sea.
meanings: It is much easier to say something than to actually do it
Making promises is easy, but keeping them is hard
Talking about a plan is very different from carrying it out
Saying is easy, doing is hard
Words are easy, actions are difficult
Good intentions often don’t turn into action
There is a big gap between what people say and what they do
englishEquivalent: Easier said than done.
englishEquivalents: Easier said than done
Talk is cheap
hints: The sea is something hard to cross.
It is often said to someone making big promises or plans.
It is about the gap between talking about something and actually doing it.

original: ድር ቢያብር አንበሳ ያስር
literal: When spider webs unite, they can tie up a lion.
meanings: When weak people unite, they can defeat something powerful
Unity gives the small great strength
Working together, the weak can overcome the strong
Together the weak can beat the strong
Many weak people together can defeat a powerful enemy
There is strength in unity
When the weak join forces they become strong
englishEquivalent: United we stand, divided we fall.
englishEquivalents: United we stand, divided we fall
Unity is strength
hints: One strand of web is nothing to a lion.
It's said to rally people against a stronger opponent.
It's about the strength of standing together.

original: Air beriak tanda tak dalam.
literal: Rippling water is a sign that it is not deep.
meanings: People who boast loudly often know little
Those who make the most noise usually have the least substance
Showing off is a sign of shallowness
Loud people are often shallow
People who boast the most know the least
Show-offs often have nothing behind them
Truly knowledgeable people are quiet
englishEquivalent: Empty vessels make the most noise.
englishEquivalents: Empty vessels make the most noise
hints: Deep water tends to be calm and still.
It's said about show-offs and loudmouths.
It's about how noisy people are often shallow.

original: Без труда не вытащишь и рыбку из пруда.
literal: Without effort you can't even pull a little fish out of a pond.
meanings: Nothing can be achieved without hard work
Even small rewards require effort
You have to work to get results
Nothing comes without effort
Hard work is needed for any reward
You can’t get anything without effort
Even easy things take work
englishEquivalent: No pain, no gain.
englishEquivalents: No pain, no gain
There’s no such thing as a free lunch
hints: A small fish in a small pond should be easy, shouldn't it?
It's said to someone hoping for results without trying.
It's about how everything worthwhile takes effort.

original: Ağaç yaşken eğilir.
literal: A tree is bent while it is still young.
meanings: It is easiest to shape and teach people when they are young
Habits and character should be formed in childhood
Teach children early, because adults are hard to change
Teach people while they are young
Children learn best when they are young
It is hard to change someone once they are grown
Good habits must be taught early
englishEquivalent: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
englishEquivalents: You can’t teach an old dog new tricks
hints: Try bending an old, thick trunk.
It's usually said about raising children.
It's about shaping people while they are young.

original: Nā tō rourou, nā taku rourou ka ora ai te iwi.
literal: With your food basket and my food basket, the people will thrive.
meanings: When everyone contributes, the whole community prospers
Sharing and cooperation help everyone flourish
Each person's contribution together sustains the group
If everyone contributes, everyone benefits
Everyone working together makes the community strong
Cooperation benefits everyone
When we all share, we all do well
englishEquivalent: Many hands make light work.
englishEquivalents: Many hands make light work
hints: Neither basket alone would be enough.
It's often quoted at community gatherings and fundraisers.
It's about everyone contributing so the group can flourish.

original: 三个和尚没水喝
literal: Three monks have no water to drink.
meanings: When too many people share a job, nobody does it
Shared responsibility means no one takes responsibility
More people can mean less gets done because everyone leaves it to others
Too many people means nobody does the work
When everyone is responsible, nobody does it
If many people share a job, each waits for the others
Too many people and the work never gets done
englishEquivalent: Too many cooks spoil the broth. / Everybody's business is nobody's business.
englishEquivalents: Too many cooks spoil the broth
Everybody’s business is nobody’s business
hints: One monk alone would simply fetch the water himself.
With three, each one waits for another to go.
It's about how shared responsibility can mean nobody does the work.

original: ایک اور ایک گیارہ
literal: One and one make eleven.
meanings: Two people working together achieve far more than each alone
Unity multiplies strength
Teamwork makes people much stronger
Together we are stronger
Working together is better than working alone
Unity makes you much stronger
Two people together can do far more than twice as much
englishEquivalent: Two heads are better than one.
englishEquivalents: Two heads are better than one
Unity is strength
hints: Picture the two digits written side by side.
It's about what happens when two people join forces.
It's about cooperation making you far stronger than the sum of the parts.

original: Ang hindi lumingon sa pinanggalingan ay hindi makararating sa paroroonan.
literal: One who does not look back at where they came from will not reach where they are going.
meanings: Never forget your roots or the people who helped you
Remembering your origins is necessary for success
You should honour your past and humble beginnings
Remember where you came from
Respect where you came from
Stay humble and remember your origins
Don’t forget the people who helped you get where you are
englishEquivalent: Don't forget your roots.
englishEquivalents: Don’t forget your roots
Never forget where you came from
hints: This isn't about directions on a road.
